speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is my honour to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 106 from a number of western Canadians who are concerned about the Government's intentions to change the Patent Act relating to prescription drugs which they believe will increase drug prices for Canadian consumers and will severely restrict the ability of average Canadians to purchase those necessary prescription drugs. subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CHANGES TO PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition certified by the Clerk of Petitions on December 15, 1986. I regret that it has taken so long to present it to the House of Commons but there have been so many petitions to present on this particular issue. I am glad the Parliamentary Secretary gave us the chance to point that out.
In their petition these Canadians have indicated their concern that the Government intends to change the Patent Act. They expect that this will result in higher costs, not only for provincial government plans, but for those people who because of their health needs are required to purchase prescription drugs on an ongoing basis. They also believe that this is yet another example of the Canadian Government making concessions to the United States in the free trade talks at the expense of average Canadians. Therefore, your petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to reject those proposals which will increase prescription drug prices for Canadians.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CANADA POST CORPORATION PLAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too have the honour to present to the House hundreds of petitions from various regions all over the country, denouncing the new corporate plan of the Canada Post Corporation that creates two classes of citizens with the permanent installation of superboxes in urban as well as rural areas. The petitioners state that closing rural post offices deprives citizens of a unique federal presence and reduces vital postal services in rural areas, and the raise in postal rates, particularly on second-class mail, jeopardizes the distribution of numerous weekly and regional newspapers, magazines, and so on.
Your petitioners humbly pray that Parliament will reject the plan of Canada Post and urge it to deliver mail to all Canadian citizens without distinction.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is really too bad that the very first time I have a chance to speak to the Budget, I have to admit the Budget is a big zero as far as Canadian taxpayers are concerned. When I say a big zero, I am of course referring to the quality of the Budget that was brought down and to the impact this Budget will have on the taxpayer's purse. And that is why the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), seconded by the Hon. Member
The Budget-Mr. Grondin
for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), proposed the following amendment to the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson):
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"this House condemns the government for:
-presenting a budget that increases taxes on individual Canadians for the third year in a row, totalling billions and billions of dollars;
-widening the gap between the rich and the poor by their ill-advised and heartless fiscal policy;
-cutting the crucial Regional Economic Development budget, for the third year in a row; and
-once again delaying the long promised essential tax reform program thereby postponing any attempt to create more fairness in our tax system which is being eroded under the present conservative administration."
Mr. Speaker, this amendment, which will be put to a vote today, in effect condemns the policies announced and the statements made before this House by the Minister of Finance.
It is often said that the Budget is a reflection of the Government's general policies, and on February 18 there was absolutely nothing in the Budget, so I think we must ask ourselves what the policies of this Government really are.
I was astonished, disappointed and almost shocked to hear the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) tell the House that with a Budget like this one, the Conservative Government knew where it was going. I have to say the Minister of Finance certainly did nothing to help the Conservative Members and Ministers who, so far, have been trying to justify the Government's position with respect to the Budget or so-called Budget that was brought down.
We of the Liberal Party also know where the Conservative Members and Ministers opposite are going. The people of Canada are judging them and will continue to judge them in the months to come, and we know where the present Progressive Conservative caucus will be after the next general election, and it will not be in Ottawa.
Actually, one wonders about the Minister of State for Youth who seems to go to considerable lengths to accept and even praise the performance of his Minister of Finance, especially when we realize that never at any time in his response or speech on the Budget did the Minister of State for Youth mention the word "youth" or the word "young", and why should he, since the Budget contains nothing for young people. That is perhaps why the Minister has tried to publish some very interesting-looking and nicely presented booklets that unfortunately contain information that has no connection with and does not reflect the policies of a responsible Government.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has failed to live up to the promises it made in its previous Budget, the one brought down on February 26, 1986, in which the Minister of Finance said: "In my next Budget, I intend to propose further measures to reform our system of social expenditures and related tax provisions." Unfortunately, the Government appears to have reneged on this commitment to social program reform. We need merely refer to the many complaints and

March 17, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Grondin
expressions of discontent we are receiving from people who were promised this, that and the other, and in my own riding, during the campaign before the by-election to replace my predecessor in the House of Commons, during which the Government party was promising rose gardens right and left, among others that it would be possible to make them eligible for benefits under the Program for Worker Adjustment even if this were to require some stickhandling. After the elections, unfortunately these people find themselves in a situation where they cannot possibly be eligible for such benefits, and of course they are very disappointed and furious about the attitude of the Conservative Government.
And then of course there are the great many Canadians who had been told they could apply for unemployment insurance benefits if they opted for early retirement. Particularly in our region, quite a few people did apply under this program, looking forward to early retirement because they were convinced they would be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Many of these early retirees are quite disillusioned and upset because the Government has failed to live up to its promise.
1 doubt that the average Canadian is strongly opposed to some kind of reform of social programs, but they ought to be more effective and take current conditions into consideration. Like my colleague the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau), our finance critic, I think a guaranteed annual income system should have been set up long ago. We passed a resolution to that effect at our November Party convention, so we will be in a position to do something about it after the next general elections when we are called upon to form the new Government.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to recall some of the points raised by my colleague, the Opposition finance critic, in the remarks he made recently. He was referring to the gap between rich and poor Canadians after the three Conservative budgets, and he went on to single out the situation of young people. There is nothing at all in this Budget to meet the needs of unemployed youths. Nor is there anything flowing from the commitment made by the Prime Minister of Canada at last year's provincial premiers conference in Vancouver when he promised to set up a child care program. Mr. Speaker, Canadian families will just have to carry a much heavier tax load than what they have been used to this far. Mr. Speaker, does it make sense that, as a result of the 1987 Budget, a working married couple with two children should be taxed $966 more than in 1984? Or that a married couple with two children and only one breadwinner earning $30,000 be asked to pay $1,020 more than in 1984? We could go on and on like this, but such figures are so depressing that we would rather not.
As could be expected, the Government did not dare tamper with the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption because this would have been a direct blow to Party supporters.
Nor did the Government do anything about big business because, here again, the friends of the Party would have been hard hit. As I see it, any Government should make sure that companies and businesses pay their fair share of taxes. Since 1984, unfortunately, 90 per cent of new taxes have been levied
against individual Canadians while corporations have had to come up with a little less than 9 per cent. The least I can say is that this is unfair to the average taxpayer.
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government is facing a couple of problems: Canadians are not fooled, and this Government will not be re-elected two years from now. Again referring to what is generally happening to young people, throughout his Budget speech the Minister of Finance did not once utter the word "youth". As Young Liberals of Canada President Jonathan Scheiderman put it, it would seem that the Conservative Party solution to the unemployment of young people is to let them grow older. If we are to believe what the Minister of Finance said in his May 23, 1985 Budget speech, it is an ongoing priority of this Government to encourage a much-improved research and development performance in Canada. Unfortunately, since the Conservatives have been in power, the amounts allocated to the National Research Council have decreased from $520 million in 1984 to $398 million in 1986, and an additional cut-back of $20 million was announced in October 1986. How can we believe in research development when the Government is reducing the amounts allocated to this activity in its Budget?
The way the Government is treating the Ministry of Youth is a perfect illustration of the priority given to the problems of young people. The Government has cut back over $200 million from youth programs since 1984. It is hard to understand the self-sastisfaction of the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) when he is asked questions about these cut-backs. When the most important initiative aimed at Canadian youth is the new tax on chips and granola bars, how can young people have confidence in the Government? It has never shown the least concern for future generations, as Mr. Schneiderman said quite recently.
Since the Government did away with the Katimavik program, we have often been told that programs to solve the problems of young people will be introduced in due time. Yet, Katimavik was abolished over a year ago and the Government has yet to announce something to replace it, except for some minor programs which fall quite a bit short of Katimavik in giving real experience and training to young people. If the Budget is not the proper place to announce new programs, will the Minister of Finance one day tell young Canadians when it will be time to introduce the marvellous programs promised by the Conservative Government? Indeed, when will young people stop being treated like third-class citizens by this Government?
Quite recently, the Department of Employment and Immigration sent us information on the amounts allocated to job creation programs for young people. This information shows the amounts allocated in 1985-86 and 1986-87. According to this information, in 1985-86, $673.2 million were allocated to job creation for young people and 253,400 young people took part in the various programs. For the current fiscal year, 1986-87, the estimates show that $720.3 million will be allocated and that 230,000 young people will take part. This is according to the figures we have been given. It is difficult to reconcile the fact that, while the Government is saying that
March 17, 1987

$47.1 million more will be allocated to these job creation programs, 23,200 fewer young Canadians will be able to participate in them.
In the list of federal, provincial and territorial programs Youth Affairs 1986-87, which is an official document distributed throughout Canada by Employment and Immigration and used regularly by the directors of Canada Manpower Centres, a whole section is devoted to federal job-creation programs. This document is used by job counsellors in campus employment centres and Canada employment centres for students, as well as by young people themselves. If we compare this official document and the Canadian Job Strategy information provided by Employment and Immigration, we note many differences both in the job-creation programs themselves and in the amounts allocated to these programs. How can there be any coherence in the youth policy of this Conservative Government? For instance, the Section 38 program appears in the Canadian Job Strategy table, but cannot be found in the index of federal programs. In the case of the Skill Shortage program, which is related to shortages of specialized workers, the index shows that the amount allocated for young people was $4.5 million in 1985-86, while the data provided by Employment and Immigration gives a figure of $24.7 million.
In the case of job development, in the index, the total budget shown is $239.4 million while the data provided by Employment and Immigration show the amount allocated to young people alone as $308.8 million. Where is the coherence, Mr. Speaker? Where is the transparency?
To return to the Hot 100 publication, an abridged guide to the Canadian Government's youth grants and services, that publication in itself is an excellent initiative. Young Canadians needed a guide to find their way around the programs and services set up by the Canadian Government. However, its content is highly questionable.
First, upon reading the guide, one very soon realizes that a very large majority of programs listed were already in force under the Liberal administration. New programs are very scarce, and, besides, it is clear from many of the listed programs and services that the Minister used this as some sort of a carryall to convey an impression that his Government's programs and services were very numerous, although many of them are seldomly used, of little interest to the young or have not really been designed for them.
Besides, program and service descriptions are so short that their nature and requirements are totally or partly left out. Among the programs and services listed in Hot 100 that were not really designed for the young, there is the Hotline services of the Small Business Secretariat, the FDB's management seminars, the business counselling, the video clinics on management, the FDB's information services, community development, the Federal Business Development Bank's booklet Minding Your Own Business, the Equipment Management internal officer and Probationer Program. Also included are programs of such a general nature as health insurance and
The Budget-Mr. Grondin
unemployment insurance, the Canada public insurance plan, family allowances, the missing children programs, the Canada Pension Plan, Federal assistance to post-secondary education, and so on and so forth.
This Government, Mr. Speaker, is constantly bragging about its youth employment policy and its funding. It would indeed be interesting to know about that policy. However, there is nowhere to be found a detailed profile of the policy explaining the details of the various programs, nor the specific budgets allocated. It is no surprise to me that over the weekend, the Minister of State for Youth should have announced, when promoting Hot 100, that according to a report in La Presse, he was shying away from a youth policy, since a youth policy never has been a feature, or a concern, or a priority of the Tory Government.
It would be important for the Government to develop a policy, and that such a policy be made available as one complete and explicit official document, if ever it comes to light.
Mr. Speaker, we are entitled to ask at which point would this Government consider the young for what they are and at their fair value? When will he give any priority to that major group, the leaders of tomorrow, that accounts for 22.6 per cent of Canada's labour force?
Research and development expenditures should increase by 4 per cent in 1986, as compared with 12 per cent and 11 per cent in 1985. Expenditures for 1986 amounted to 1.3 per cent of Canada's gross national product, which is much less than the 2.5 per cent spent in the United States and 2.7 per cent in Japan. However, during the 1984 election, the Progressive Conservative Government was committed to doubling research and development funding over the next four years in order to bring it to 2.5 per cent of the gross national product. It is that sort of statement and promise that has brought this Government to power but is today disheartening our people and driving them into rejecting this Government that has no respect whatsoever for its commitments and does not intend to honour them, if we are to rely on the figures that were published and that lead us to believe that this Government intends to follow along the same line it has been promoting since 1984.
Where employment centres are concerned, it is unfortunate to note that a drastic reduction in staff is expected, a staff that has proved to be very useful on campus in our colleges and universities but unfortunately the Government has decided to reduce the staff on duty in our various Canadian colleges and universities.
Surely, we could speak at length, Mr. Speaker, but I see that the time allotted to me is almost over but I would like to say that at the post-secondary level, by tabling such a budget the government is only fuelling the opposition shown not merely on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker, but throughout Canada.

March 17, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Vincent
Those Canadians are voicing their views through Gallup polls and briefs, at meetings on social occasions, and they have all kinds of responses which indicate beyond any shadow of a doubt that they are getting ready for an outright firing of all the Tory Members who approved that budget and failed to take into account, at least as far as I am concerned, that extremely important segment of the population which represents 22.6 per cent of Canadians and which will in the years ahead take over from us, and I mean our young people. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that it is too late for the Government to reverse its action, but it is not too late to at least launch programs which would show that this Government still has a heart and that it can be truly concerned about our young people and not solely about the friends of the party.

Mr. Speaker, having heard the speech made by their elected representative the people in the Saint-Maurice riding must be very disappointed today in view of the fact that he spent half of his time saying that the Conservative Government would not be re-elected and the other half reading remarks made by other Hon. Members or quoting from this or that. I am very sad when I see my honourable friend from Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) behave this way.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring up again some of the points he tried to make. I honestly believed that the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice knew what a budget is. I realize now that he does not have the faintest idea of what it is. A budget is the financial statement of a country which must be tabled once a year.
As his deskmate the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard- Anjou (Mr. Gagliano), the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice thinks that a budget should provide the Minister of Finance with the opportunity to announce what each and every department is planning to do during the forthcoming year. He mentioned what he felt should have been announced concerning the young people of this country, but he forgot to mention what my honourable colleague has done for women; he forgot to deal with regional development; he forgot all of that because a budget is based on detailed estimates of planned or expected expenditures.
The Department of Finance does not have to make announcements in the Budget. For instance, what would have happened last year, when Western Canadians farmers urgently needed assistance had the Government refused arguing that the Opposition did not want any announcements at that particular time but that instead they should appear in the Budget. Wait a while; in the Budget we will announce what in
fact you need now. I do not think that Western Canada farmers would have been happy, Mr. Speaker. That is what the Opposition does not understand. The Budget provides each and every Department with the funding it needs, and it is up to each Minister during the year to make the necessary announcements pertaining to their respective areas of responsibility.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member referred to young Canadians. What had the previous Government done for them? We have reduced the unemployment rate among young Canadians by 3 per cent. We have still a long way to go, but at least we have done something, contrary to the previous Government which simply allowed the unemployment rate among young Canadians to rise. He referred to the very good booklet published by the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest). This booklet has been very well received everywhere in Canada, except in the ridings held by the Opposition. So, Mr. Speaker, you can see how that works.
As far as the social programs reform is concerned, a few things have been accomplished. The Hon. Member failed to mention the Federal sales tax credit which the Government has implemented to help low income people. The promise which the Prime Minister made last week concerning day-care centres will become a reality. Please, be patient.
The Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice did not mention- which surprises me, for I know him to be straightforward and honest-the minimum income tax which was established in January 1986, although his leader was definitely against imposing a minimum tax on high income people. He did not mention that, Mr. Speaker. On the other hand, he talked a lot about corporations which do not pay a cent in income tax. Mr. Speaker, we owe this income tax system to the Liberal Party which governed this country for 20 years, but the Hon. Member failed to mention the changes we have made and the steps we have taken over the past two years to eliminate a great many tax loopholes. He mentioned the cuts concerning the National Research Council. It is those people who made up the previous Government and who are now sitting in the Opposition who set up the scientific research tax credit which caused billions of dollars to be wasted, an abused tax credit we had to get rid of. Billions have been spent under their policy, and you have seen the magazine Actualite . . . when he speaks about friends of the Government, we should not forget either all these lawyers of Liberal allegiance who profited from that scientific research tax credit, or all the companies which also benefited from it. Anyway, Mr. Speaker, here lies the difference between the Conservative Government and the previous Liberal Government: we work at the national level, we work to help people throughout the country and each and every Conservative Member in this House is working for the people of his or her riding. We do not work only to be re-elected, and our policies in particular are designed to improve the well-being of Canadians and not just to win the next election, as the previous Liberal Government used to do. I must say, Mr. Speaker, that they did succeed on that point. One cannot hold it against them, since their image was not too bad and they succeeded in being re-elected. But that is not what is important. What is important is that nationally and internationally, Canada take the place it deserves, and this has happened only since 1984.
Let me refer to other comments of the Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice. He spoke about the capital gain tax exemption.
Mr. Speaker, that is a good provision which has proved itself up to now as far as the economy and job creation are concerned. When 1 am told that it is meant to help the Government's friends, I think there are more wealthy people on the Liberal side than on the Conservative side. So let them not tell me this kind of story. They have been in power for 20 years and have made the most of it. Let them not tell me that wealthy people are only on the Conservative side. Mr. Speaker, this I suggest is only playing politics and in so doing, my colleague from the riding of Saint-Maurice (Mr. Grondin) has somewhat disappointed me.
He spoke as well about youth programs. The Challenge Program has created more jobs with less money because it has been carried out efficiently. But what is still more important, young people in 1985, 1986 and again in 1987, will have had during the summer months the opportunity not just to work but also to work in their own fields of endeavour, as against the former Summer Canada programs, or whatever their name was, under which summer work for students meant lawn mowing and house painting and all that sort of informative activities. No, Mr. Speaker, since 1984 young Canadians have been working during summer in their own fields, and I could quote testimonies from people in the Trois-Rivieres riding, from young people in my riding, who think the program is great because it gave them a chance to work for four months in their respective areas of competence, and that is something new because it never did exist under the former Liberal regime.
So we need no lessons from anybody in that regard.
The Hon. Member said that the Conservative Government was elected on its promises. No, Mr. Speaker, this Government was elected because Canadians were fed up with the policies, not to say the petty politics, of the former Liberal administration. It must be recalled, Mr. Speaker, that they were elected in 1980 on the promise that they would not increase the tax on gasoline by 18 cents a gallon. One year later we had twice that increase, Mr. Speaker. When we came to power in September 1984, the price of gasoline in Trois-Rivieres was 60 cents a litre, Mr. Speaker, whereas it is now 50 cents. The price of

March 17, 1987
The Budget-Mr. Vincent
gasoline has been reduced thanks to the energy policies of the Conservative Government. And in the riding of Saint-Maurice, the price of gaz has also decreased. I have the opportunity to go there once in a while, and I know it, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The price of gas has decreased, but no thanks to you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And once again, 1 suppose that if interest rates have gone down, it is not because of the judicious policies of the Conservative Government. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And the small- and medium-size businesses . .. You can see Mr. Speaker, that the truth hurts. Lately, I had the opportunity to visit in the riding of Saint-Maurice some small- and medium-size businesses which are doing very well. In Trois-Rivieres also, they are doing quite well, small- and medium-size, they are expanding and people are proud of our policies. In Trois-Rivieres our small- and medium-size business people realize that with a Conservative Government they save $1,000 in interest a year. These are tangible achievements the people can see when they get money in their pockets.
Mr. Speaker, personal income has increased by 5 per cent since we have been in power. These are positive achievements. The number of small- and medium-size businesses has increased by 13 per cent. It is not only job creation. Canadian entrepreneurship, now aware of its potential, is moving ahead with the help of the Conservative Government. After being crushed as a result of Liberal policies, as you know, Mr. Speaker. All these achievements are the reason why we have a Budget that everybody, except the Opposition, considers excellent. We are only criticized for not having reduced the deficit further and I can understand that. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, you know that 50 per cent of the expenditures in this budget have to do with social programs. Twenty-five per cent are for interest payments on their debt. Twenty-five per cent of public expenditures in 1987-1988 go towards interest payments on debts incurred by the former liberal administration. We have to live with that, Mr. Speaker. We have no choice.
They spent carelessly and haphazardly, without regard for the proper use of funds. I spoke earlier of scientific research. I could mention a multitude of job creation programs which were a farce, which were tailor-made for friends and acquaintances, which provided temporary jobs, Mr. Speaker, if any at all. And I could go on at length.
With regard to Quebec, Mr. Speaker, what this Government has accomplished over the last two years is tremendous. Worthy of note are the CF-18 contract, the Hyundai plant, the step forward in agricultural policy, Mr. Speaker, amounting to a billion and a half dollars over five years. For five years, the former administration had denied our dairy producers what they rightly deserved. We came up with a solution in 1985, Mr. Speaker, less than one year after having been elected. And I know for a fact that the Hon. Member for Beauce (Mr. Bernier) was totally in favor of this initiative. The unemployment rate has declined.
A record number of agreements have been signed between the federal Government and the Province of Quebec in the fields of science and technology, regional development, transport, to name but a few, Mr. Speaker, agreements which have notably benefited Trois-Rivieres-in the area of transport, Mr. Speaker, since $18 million are to be spent to renovate the Trois-Rivieres bridge. These positive accomplishments have been brought about by the Federal Government, in co-operation with the Government of Quebec. The press mentioned this morning that the time for bickering between the Federal and Provincial Governments had ended, Mr. Speaker. Prior to my entry in the political arena, there was a time when the provincial member and federal member never spoke to one another other than through the press. The Member for Trois-Rivieres and the Member for Saint-Maurice did not speak to one another except through the press. That is not the way things are done today, Mr. Speaker. We work in co-operation with the province. I work in co-operation with my two provincial colleagues, and it works well in the area. This is what I call team work, this is what I call the national reconciliation the Prime Minister had promised and we have brought.
Mr. Speaker, there is one question to which I would like an Hon. Member on the other side of the House to answer. In 1983-84, we had a deficit of $32 billion. We came in power in 1984, as you know, Mr. Speaker, and we said in the November 1984 Economic Statement: we cut a bit everywhere, because we have to put some order in our own house and then see where we are going. We still had a $38 billion deficit. Mr. Speaker, $6 billion were spent before the election. Where did that money go? I could give you examples, I have some in my own riding. They sprinkled a little bit of money just about everywhere in order to win. But the Canadian people did not go along this time. They understood in 1984 that you do not win the heart of Quebecers by spending a lot of money; in the riding of Trois-Rivieres, in the riding of Beauce, in the riding of Labelle, it is won over by the Conservative Government-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And in the riding of Rimouski.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the riding of Rimouski too, of course. And I feel sorry for you, Liberals, in the next election; you are going to try to win those ridings, but because people are proud of their Hon. Members and work with them, and because they acknowledge that their Hon. Members fight for Quebec and for their ridings-
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion I would like to say that this is the first time in 30 years that the federal deficit will be reduced for three consecutive years, the first time in 30 years, Mr. Speaker. That is to say, the last time it happened, I was one year old. That was a long time ago, Mr. Speaker. Thanks to whom? Again, thanks to the great policies of the Prime Minister, of the Minister of Finance and of the whole Conservative caucus.
March 17, 1987

Mr. Speaker, I could say a lot more about this excellent budget, and I would ask Hon. Members to support the motion put forth by Minister Wilson, and of course reject the Opposition motion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. I will start with one, in order to give a chance to other Members. And anyway, this is a question I had already asked during the debate on the borrowing authority legislation. He stated that the Liberals wasted $6 billion before the elections, because when they came to power they found themselves with a S38 billion deficit, and that this Conservative Government has been reducing the deficit year after year. First, I would like to tell him that this is not quite the truth, because, last year, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had proposed a $29.5 billion deficit and we now get a $32 billion deficit that is equal to the last budget's last deficit, the last full deficit under the Liberal administration, that is $32 billion in 1983-84. So there is no reduction from three years ago. But in 1984-85 and 1985-86, there still was an increase of some $6 billion in tax receipts. Yet, the deficit at the end of 1986 is the same. Now, could he tell me-I believe he has had the time to figure it out and look at it-where those $6 billion have gone and how it is that after increasing taxes by $6 billion since they came to power, the deficit at the end of 1986 is $32 billion, just as it was in 1984?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my colleague the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) for his question. When we took over, the deficit reached $38 billion. The first year, we brought it down to $34 billion, the following year to $32 billion, and this year to $29 billion. I suggest we have done a very good job.
Unfortunately, the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard- Anjou does not seem to know that the cost of social programs increases every year. For instance, Mr. Speaker, Old Age Security Pension benefits, family allowances, and transfer payments to the provinces are increasing. While it is true that Government revenues have increased, so have expenses. This is simple mathematics and if my hon. friend wants to be honest, he will have to admit that transfer payments to the provinces and social program benefits are responsible to a large extent for the increase in Government spending. He should not forget the debts incurred by the previous Government and which we must pay back. Interest payments on a debt do not go down when the debt is increasing; they grow and must be paid. They are responsible for the increase in our spending.
The Conservative Government currently administers the country with approximately 25 per cent of the overall government budget. International agreements which were signed before we came to power and which we all agree have to be adhered to, namely those concerning National Defence and CIDA. There are increases there too. There has been very little increase, if any, in the expenses which the Government
The Budget-Mr. Vincent
controls. That is not where the increase is occurring. Revenues must increase, because the remaining expenses are increasing.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to tell my colleague from Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent) that he is right to say that we see budgets differently. That is obvious. First, the Budget was brought down in the House, and then we were told about the expenditures projected by the Government for the coming year. We were then able to see that there is a relationship between the Budget and the Main Estimates for 1987-88, and this relationship gave us food for thought. Of course, everything that we had expected after the Budget was brought down was later confirmed by the Main Estimates.
Where I disagree with my colleague from Trois-Rivieres is when he says that I simply read what had been written by other people and spent my time saying that the Government would not be re-elected. I think there is some truth in the latter, and as for his claim that what I said was written by others, we could hardly be expected to speak to a variety of issues since the Budget failed to reflect any specific policies or make positive forecasts for Canada's future.
And I don't think that my answers to questions or what I was able to contribute on the youth problem and the total absence of any policies or forecasts in this respect, I don't think this was mentioned by anyone else, Mr. Speaker, since even the Minister of State for Youth, in his speech on the Budget, never mentioned the word "young" or "youth". And why should he, since there was absolutely nothing in the Budget for young people.
As for Hot 100, I simply want to say to the Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres that the layout is very good, and I said as much in my speech. The booklet is put together quite well, but unfortunately, aside from certain programs that existed before, if we look for programs that were introduced by the Conservative Government since 1984, I'm afraid the Hon. Member will have to admit they were conspicuous by their absence from this publication.
As far as Challenge '87, Challenge '86, or Challenge '85 go, I do not think my colleague can accuse me of ever having spoken against this program. What we denounce is the Challenge program funding, in light of other increases. Among other things, I am referring to minimum wage levels in the various provinces, particularly in Ontario and Quebec this year, and to the difficulties we experienced when attempting to obtain additional funds to compensate for the extra $30 million which had been earmarked for the 1986 census summer program. These $30 million have been cut back this year and, no matter what my colleague from Trois-Rivieres may say, it translates into so many fewer jobs. Fewer jobs will be available this year, unless they plan to reduce the salaries to be paid to young people hired under the Challenge '87 program.

March 17, 1987
The Budget-Mr. de Jong
All things considered, Mr. Speaker, that is a sharp reduction and we cannot accept that young people be penalized by a Government which could not care less about this group that makes up 22.6 per cent of the Canadian population.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try again. It doesn't seem to sink in. The Budget is not an instrument for giving away goodies to certain groups in our society. The Budget provides certain sums of money for each department, and it is up to the responsible Minister to spend that money in the course of the year. The Minister of State for Youth will make his own announcements when appropriate. It is not up to the Minister of Finance to announce in the Budget what is going to be done for our youth this year. And I see my colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight). There was nothing in the Budget about Indian Affairs. However, in the months to come, the Minister will be making announcements that concern Indians. That is what the Hon. Member fails to understand, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to point out that for the first time in twenty years, a Government has given a forecast of its expenditures and at the end of the year, the forecast has proved to be correct, and we have been doing this for three years running. It is the first time, Mr. Speaker. It involves administering the country like Canadians administer their family budget and like companies administer theirs. When they say: We are going to spend X thousand dollars this year, they spend X thousand dollars. For twenty years, the Liberal Government failed to balance its budget. We, Mr. Speaker, have done so, and I think that is important.
Finally, I can assure the House that the Minister of State for Youth is doing excellent work for our young people and that he has the support of the Quebec caucus and the national caucus in this respect.
